Please polish the following text to make it more eloquent and professional, keeping all original information unchanged:

LONDON, England (CNN) -- Leading British Cabinet minister Jacqui Smith's political future is in doubt after her husband admitted to paying for adult movies with taxpayers' money. Jacqui Smith surrounded by media outside her sister's home, whom she lives with in London. The home secretary's husband, Richard Timney, has apologized for the "embarrassment" he caused his wife, while she has promised to repay the money spent, including the £10 ($14) charge for the two films, the British Press Association reported. According to British media reports, Smith had not seen the videos and was "mortified" that they had "mistakenly" been paid for using her MP's expense account. Timney, who Smith pays £40,000 ($56,000) a year to be her office manager, submitted an expense claim last June for a £67 ($95) Virgin Media bill for television services in the couple's family home in Redditch, Smith's constituency, The Guardian newspaper reported. It reported the bill included two adult films, at a cost of £5 ($7) each, as well as two viewings of the heist movie "Ocean's 13" and one of "Surf's Up," a children's film about a  penguin. The revelations could not come at a worse time for Smith, who is already being investigated by the Parliamentary Commissioner for Standards over her decision to claim at least £116,000 ($164,000) in second-home allowances for her family home since becoming an MP. She has claimed the second-home allowance for her family home while living with her sister in London. Smith designated her sister's house as her "main" residence, allowing her to claim the money for her family home. Conservative and opposition leader David Cameron described the latest news as "deeply embarrassing" for Smith. He said Smith had "questions to answer," PA reported. "I do not think this individual thing is the issue. I think she has got some questions to answer about the second home issue. It does seem to me pretty incredible to claim that the home where her family is, that is not her main home. "I think this goes to a deeper problem, which is the second home allowance for MPs. The prime minister has ordered a review but he has sort of kicked it into the long grass. "The review doesn't start until September, it is not going to report until after the next election. That is hopeless. We have got to get on with it." Prime Minister Gordon Brown defended Smith. "The home secretary is doing a great job and I do not think this issue should be allowed to detract from everything she is doing to ensure we protect the public and keep our neighborhoods safe," he said. "She has done the right thing by taking steps to rectify the mistake that was made as soon as she became aware of it. "This is very much a personal matter for Jacqui. She has made her apology, her husband has made clear that he has apologized." Last week Brown ordered a review of the complex and opaque system of MPs' pay and allowances. Do you think Smith should resign?

# BREAKING NEWS: Jacqui Smith apologises after taxpayer-funded expenses claim includes adult films

**LONDON — March 29, 2009** — Home Secretary Jacqui Smith is facing intense political pressure after it emerged that a Virgin Media bill submitted through her parliamentary expenses included charges for two adult films watched by her husband.

The films, reportedly costing **£5 each**, appeared on a household communications bill claimed against Smith’s parliamentary allowances. Her husband, Richard Timney, acknowledged that he had ordered the films while Smith was away and issued a public apology for causing her embarrassment.

Smith said the charges had been included inadvertently and promised to repay the amount.

> “I am sorry that in claiming for my internet connection, I mistakenly claimed for a television package alongside it,” she said. “As soon as the matter was brought to my attention, I took immediate steps to contact the relevant parliamentary authorities and rectify the situation.”

The episode is politically damaging not primarily because of the modest sum involved, but because it reinforces growing public anger over MPs’ use of taxpayer-funded allowances.

## Virgin Media package placed under scrutiny

The disputed charges formed part of a broader Virgin Media bill covering services such as internet access, telephone use and television. Parliamentary rules allowed MPs to claim costs necessary for carrying out their duties, including certain communications expenses, but personal entertainment was not an allowable expense.

Smith’s office maintained that the television component had been bundled with services used for parliamentary work and that the inclusion of the films was an oversight rather than an intentional attempt to make taxpayers pay for private viewing.

Nevertheless, the adult-film detail transformed what might otherwise have been a minor accounting dispute into a major national story. Opposition politicians and taxpayer groups argued that senior ministers had a particular responsibility to examine claims before submitting them.

Timney, who was also employed as Smith’s parliamentary assistant, said:

> “I am really sorry for any embarrassment I have caused Jacqui. I can fully understand why people might be angry and offended by this.”

## Controversy compounds second-home questions

The revelation comes while Smith is already under examination over her housing expenses.

She had designated a room in her sister’s London home as her main residence for parliamentary purposes. That enabled her to claim second-home allowances for the family house in her Redditch constituency, where her husband and children lived.

Smith argued that the designation complied with parliamentary rules because she spent much of the week in London while Parliament was sitting. Critics, however, questioned whether her sister’s property could reasonably be regarded as her principal home when her family residence was in Redditch.

The Parliamentary Commissioner for Standards subsequently investigated the arrangement. Although Smith was not found to have deliberately fabricated her living circumstances, the controversy intensified demands for reform and contributed to the perception that the expenses system allowed MPs to exploit technical rules unavailable to ordinary voters.

## Immediate threat to Smith’s authority

As Home Secretary, Smith holds one of the most senior positions in government, overseeing policing, counterterrorism, immigration and national security. The personal nature of the claim threatens to distract from that work and weaken her authority at a time when Prime Minister Gordon Brown’s government is already struggling with poor poll ratings and public distrust.

Downing Street indicated that Brown continued to support her, and there was no immediate suggestion that she would be dismissed over the bill alone. However, the affair placed her political judgment under renewed scrutiny and gave opponents an easily understood symbol of the wider expenses culture.

The key questions for Smith’s future are now:

- whether further questionable claims emerge;
- whether parliamentary authorities impose sanctions;
- whether Brown concludes that the controversy has made her position untenable;
- and how voters in her marginal Redditch constituency respond.

## Part of a wider expenses crisis

The case is likely to intensify pressure for an overhaul of Parliament’s allowances system. MPs’ claims had long been processed with limited transparency, allowing expenses to be approved even when they appeared politically indefensible.

The distinction between what was technically permitted and what the public considered reasonable was rapidly becoming impossible for party leaders to ignore. Smith’s case was especially potent because the expense involved private entertainment and because she was a Cabinet minister responsible for enforcing the law.

The immediate financial loss to the taxpayer was small. The reputational cost was far greater.

## Impact on her political future

The Virgin Media disclosure did not, by itself, immediately end Smith’s Cabinet career. But it became one of the most memorable episodes of the expenses scandal and deepened the damage caused by the dispute over her homes.

Smith left the post of Home Secretary in **June 2009**, during Brown’s reshuffle, after making clear that she expected to return to the back benches. Her departure came amid broader political turmoil and the nationwide parliamentary-expenses crisis, so it would be misleading to attribute it solely to the adult-film charges. Nonetheless, the Virgin Media story severely undermined her standing and made her continued presence in the Cabinet more difficult.

At the **2010 general election**, Smith lost Redditch to Conservative candidate Karen Lumley. National dissatisfaction with Labour, the marginal nature of the constituency and the expenses scandal all contributed to the defeat.

The affair therefore became a defining moment in Smith’s career: a £10 personal charge, mistakenly passed to the taxpayer, helped crystallise a much larger controversy about judgment, privilege and accountability—and damaged the prospects of one of Labour’s most senior politicians.
